name: Queretaro de Arteaga
summary_text: A split record: Querétaro's congress banned conversion practices on 29 June 2023 with penalties of 2-6 years, yet it is one of six states Human Rights Watch (March 2025) lists as having never legislated any legal-gender-recognition procedure, leaving trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched. No state-specific incident or enforcement evidence was identified.

sources.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (no cached copy); Human Rights Watch news backgrounder (31 March 2025) on progress and challenges for trans rights in Mexico - the dossier cites it for the count that 22 of 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by March 2025, and for the per-state compliance picture.

sources.title: “I Just Want to Contribute to Society”: The Need for Legal Gender Recognition in Tabasco, Mexico | HRW
sources.claim_summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (no cached copy); Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) on the need for legal gender recognition in Tabasco state - it documents that the absence of any gender-recognition procedure exposes trans people to police and institutional mistreatment, co-authored with a local trans community organisation; the dossier cites it as the clearest case among the six states whose legislatures still refuse any procedure.

sources.title: Transfemicide becomes a crime in a ‘watershed’ moment for Mexico City | Transgender | The Guardian
sources.claim_summary: Guardian report (24 July 2024) on Mexico City making transfeminicide a crime with sentences of up to 70 years (the 'Paola Buenrostro law', named for a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose attacker was released after 48 hours despite footage and witnesses and has been on the run since): Mexico City is the second of the country's 32 states to criminalise transfeminicide - earlier in 2024 Nayarit, a small Pacific-coast state, introduced sentences of up to 60 years for the crime; the law also lets victims' friends, not only relatives, claim bodies and drive investigations, which matters where families disown trans relatives; it lands against more than 95% impunity for homicides in Mexico in 2022, believed higher for transfeminicides.
